tip.title: Decide when and where, in advance
tip.why: A 2006 meta-analysis of 94 studies found that people who wrote an if-then plan, such as 'when I finish lunch, I will go for a walk', were considerably more likely to follow through than people who only set a goal. The plan hands the decision to a cue in your day so you don't have to find willpower in the moment.
how: Pick one thing you keep meaning to do.
Write it as 'When X happens, I will do Y', with X a specific time, place or event.
Put the sentence somewhere you will see it, and notice the cue when it arrives.
tip.src: Gollwitzer & Sheeran · Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 2006
tip.ask: What is one thing I could attach to a cue I already hit every day?

markets.headline: Wall Street closed its fourth straight weekly loss on Friday; chips bounced, but the S&P 500 still ended the week about 2.7% lower.
points: The S&P 500 ended Friday at 7,376.86, up 0.3% on the day but down from 7,580.07 a week earlier. The Nasdaq Composite rose 1.09% to about 24,579 and the Dow fell 0.46% to 51,285.73. Sources differ on how bad the week was: one ranks it the worst since the April 2025 tariff crash, another the worst since June.
Thursday did most of the damage: the Nasdaq fell 5.5% and the S&P 500 4.4%, the worst day for both since April 2025. Friday's chip rebound recovered a bit over a third of that drop.

Micron rose 5.12% to $690.00 after a roughly 17% fall the day before. Vertiv, a data-center power and cooling maker, rose 3.47% to $182.86 after a 14% drop on Thursday, and remains far below its 52-week high near $380.
A strong October jobs report raised the odds of a Fed rate hike and lifted the dollar, which capped the bounce. Markets are closed until Monday, so these are still Friday's numbers.

brief.lede: A quiet Sunday: Amazon is building a home robot, a humanoid directed traffic at a Chinese marathon, and bitcoin ETFs just had their worst week since June.

articles.title: Amazon builds a new home-robot team after buying Fauna
body: Amazon has quietly put together a new team to build a home robot, CNBC reported on Sunday. Job postings describe a "new-to-world robot product" meant to work alongside family members in busy, unpredictable homes, and LinkedIn profiles suggest the group was assembled this year from much of the staff behind Astro, Amazon's rolling home device, plus a roboticist hired from MIT.

CNBC said it is unclear what kind of robot the team is making or what chores it would handle. That uncertainty matters, because Amazon has two very different starting points: Astro, which has loyal fans but never found a mass market, and **Fauna Robotics**, the startup Amazon bought in March.

Fauna's first product, Sprout, is a bipedal robot about 3 feet 6 inches tall that sold for **$50,000** and was mostly aimed at research labs as a developer platform. An Amazon spokesperson told CNBC the company bought Fauna because it is committed to tackling the challenges that could unlock the personal robotics category.

The home is the hardest place for a humanoid to work. Factories and warehouses are structured, but a kitchen changes every day, and the robot must be safe around children and pets. Most humanoid money so far has gone to industrial pilots, so a company of Amazon's size aiming at the household is a signal about where it thinks the longer-term market is.

What it means: nothing here is a product yet, and Amazon has not announced one. The useful read is about talent and intent. Watch for further hiring, any Fauna shipments to outside customers, and whether the new robot is a small wheeled helper or something that walks.

articles.title: A humanoid works traffic duty at a 36,000-runner marathon in Hangzhou
body: DEEP Robotics published details on Sunday of a deployment that took place a week earlier: humanoid robots helping manage traffic at the Hangzhou Marathon on November 1. The robots, called Hangxing No. 2 and built on the company's **DR02** platform, stand about 178 cm (5 feet 10 inches) tall and were placed at four key spots around the Huanglong Sports Center.

According to the company, their jobs included watching intersections, patrolling on their own, warning people about traffic violations and answering questions from the public. The event drew more than 300,000 registrations for about **36,000 runners**, a crowd large enough to stress any road plan. At least one report said human officers still handled complicated situations.

DEEP Robotics argued that marathons are a sensible first public job for humanoids because the crowd is concentrated in time, dense and repetitive: the same corners, the same questions, for a few hours. It said the DR02 had earlier been tested in the rain around Hangzhou's West Lake district, and that it sees this as a step toward a standard model for traffic work at big races.

Treat the performance claims carefully. Almost all coverage traces back to the company's own release, and there are no independent numbers on how many violations the robots caught or how often they needed help. It is better read as a demonstration than a result.

What it means: China keeps finding public-facing roles for humanoids where a mistake is cheap and the audience is large. If the same format shows up at other races with measurable results, it could become one of the first routine municipal uses of the machines.

articles.title: OpenAI gates a hacking-grade model; Google cuts the price of AI video
body: Two launches from earlier this week, neither covered here before, show different directions for model makers. On November 5, OpenAI introduced **GPT-6 Cyber**, a model built for authorized security work such as penetration testing and exploit development. It is not a public release: access starts with vetted customers in a tier called Daybreak Red, who must verify their identity and have their use case and security practices reviewed.

OpenAI said researchers used the model to find 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox, and Mozilla's Brian Grinstead called it a "world-class cybersecurity defense model". Reports differ on how many of those flaws are patched. OpenAI also rates the model Critical for cybersecurity under its own Preparedness Framework, one step above the High rating of its predecessor, GPT-5.6 Cyber.

The company says safeguards include checks that a model's actions match the user's permissions, monitoring for newly disclosed vulnerabilities, and IP-based access limits. In its own tests the model stayed out of off-limits services 99.93% of the time without a safety prompt, and every time with one. Those are the company's figures, not independent ones.

The same day, Google made **Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash** generally available on Google Cloud and in the Gemini API. It generates video up to 15 seconds long, up from 10 in the prior version, at about **$0.07 per second** of 720p, roughly 30% less than Omni 1.1 Flash. Outputs carry an invisible SynthID watermark. Prices for other resolutions should be checked on Google's pricing page before budgeting.

What it means: the frontier is splitting into models too risky to release widely and models getting cheaper by the month. Security is where the first is happening, and cheap video is where the second is.

articles.title: Bitcoin ETFs lose $1.28 billion in a week, the most since June
body: U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs finished the week of November 2 to 6 with **$1.28 billion** of net outflows, their largest weekly total since the week ending June 26, according to Farside Investors data cited by Crypto Times. Friday alone accounted for $411.9 million. Bitcoin itself held near $76,000 on Saturday, with ETFs closed for the weekend, so the Saturday coverage still reflects Friday's flows.

BlackRock's IBIT drove most of it, with about $1.21 billion, or 94% of the week's selling. Ether funds lost another $365 million, bringing the combined bitcoin-and-ether outflow to roughly $1.65 billion. The selling came in a week when stocks fell hard and the dollar strengthened after a strong jobs report.

Analysts are watching a cluster of levels just below the price. One is around **$75,000**, a weekly pivot that also sits near the 50-week moving average, about $75,562. Another is the 200-day average at roughly $73,197. 24/7 Wall St said another week of outflows above $1 billion together with a close below that 200-day line would make an exit by big holders look more likely.
Views differ. One analyst quoted by The Coin Republic warned of a drop toward the mid-$60,000s if $75,000 fails, and said a move above about $87,000 would be needed to signal a reversal.
What it means: price has stayed steady while ETF money leaves, which suggests other buyers are absorbing the selling. Monday's flow report is the next test.

vocab.def: A very fine, light, delicate material, like spider silk; or anything that feels that thin and airy.

cards.b: Middle English; often traced to 'goose summer', the warm autumn days when floating spider silk is seen
filmy, sheer, diaphanous
cobwebs in morning light, thin fabric, or something fragile and barely there

examples: Gossamer threads of spider silk caught the low autumn sun.
She wore a gossamer scarf that moved with every breath of wind.
vocab.ex: Gossamer threads of spider silk caught the low autumn sun.

vocab.def: Relating to twilight; describing animals that are most active at dawn and dusk.

cards.b: From Latin crepusculum, 'twilight'
dusky, dim, twilit
animals like rabbits, deer and owls that move around at dawn and dusk, or any soft low light

examples: The crepuscular glow made the whole street look gold.
Rabbits are crepuscular, so the best time to spot them is just after sunrise.
vocab.ex: The crepuscular glow made the whole street look gold.

cards.b: From Latin pellucidus, from per-, 'through', and lucidus, 'shining'
limpid, transparent, lucid
water or glass you can see through, and writing or explanations that are crystal clear

examples: The pond was so pellucid he could count the stones on the bottom.
Her pellucid explanation made the whole contract make sense.
vocab.ex: The pond was so pellucid he could count the stones on the bottom.

vocab.def: A soft whispering or rustling sound.

cards.b: From Latin susurrus, 'a whisper', a word that imitates its own sound
murmur, rustle, whisper
leaves, quiet voices, or water, anything that sounds like soft whispering

examples: A susurrus of leaves followed him down the trail.
The susurrus of the crowd settled as the lights went down.
vocab.ex: A susurrus of leaves followed him down the trail.

vocab.def: The earthy smell of rain falling on dry ground.

cards.b: Coined in 1964 by two Australian scientists from Greek petra, 'stone', and ichor, the fluid in the veins of the gods
the smell of rain, wet-earth scent
the fresh smell that rises when rain hits dry soil or pavement

examples: The petrichor after the first storm made the whole street smell alive.
She opened the window just to breathe in the petrichor.
vocab.ex: The petrichor after the first storm made the whole street smell alive.

vocab.def: Cheerful, quick readiness to do something.

cards.b: From Latin alacer, 'brisk, lively'
eagerness, readiness, promptness
answering a request quickly and willingly, with some enthusiasm

examples: She accepted the invitation with alacrity.
The new hires tackled the messy project with surprising alacrity.
vocab.ex: She accepted the invitation with alacrity.

vocab.def: Sweet and smooth to hear, like a voice or piece of music that flows easily.

cards.b: From Latin mel, 'honey', and fluere, 'to flow': literally 'flowing with honey'
dulcet, silken, honeyed
voices, music or prose that sounds smooth and pleasing

examples: The radio host's mellifluous voice made even the traffic report soothing.
She read the poem in a mellifluous whisper that quieted the room.
vocab.ex: The radio host's mellifluous voice made even the traffic report soothing.

spanish.meaning: I like your friend (he's easy to get along with)
spanish.note: In Mexican Spanish 'caer bien' means that someone strikes you as likeable. It's about the person's vibe, not romance. The opposite is 'caer mal' or, more bluntly, 'caer gordo'.

dialog.en: What did you think of Luis?

dialog.es: Me cae bien tu amigo, es muy relajado.
dialog.en: I like your friend, he's very laid back.
Yeah, he always makes me laugh.

dialog.es: Invítalo otra vez, me cae bien.
dialog.en: Invite him again, I like him.

spanish.use: Say it after meeting someone you got along with, to tell a friend your first impression.

spanish.note: In Mexican Spanish, 'ya estuvo' closes something off. It can mean 'that's done', 'we're all set', or, with the right tone, 'that's enough'. Context and your voice do the work.

dialog.en: Do you still need anything from the store?
No, that's everything, thanks.
Sure? There's still time.
Yes, we're done. Let's go.

spanish.use: Say it when a task is finished, an order is complete, or you want to politely end something.

spanish.note: In Mexican Spanish, 'al rato' means 'in a while' or 'later', usually the same day. It's a loose way to say goodbye when you expect to see someone again soon.

dialog.en: I'm going to eat, shall we meet later?
Sure. What time do you finish?
Around four.
Perfect, see you in a bit.

spanish.use: Say it when you're parting ways and expect to meet again the same day.

spanish.meaning: Give me a shout / hit me up
spanish.note: In casual Mexican Spanish, 'echar un grito' means to get in touch, usually by call or message. People say it when making loose plans or ending a chat.

dialog.es: Voy a estar por tu zona el sábado.
dialog.en: I'll be in your area on Saturday.

dialog.es: ¡Qué bien! Échame un grito cuando llegues.
dialog.en: Great! Hit me up when you get here.
Okay, I'll hit you up.
Perfect, see you there.

spanish.use: Say it when you want a friend to get in touch about plans.

spanish.note: In Mexican Spanish, 'me late' means something sounds good or appeals to you, and it works for plans, ideas and offers. Its opposite is 'no me late', I'm not feeling it.

dialog.es: ¿Qué tal si cenamos en el mercado y luego caminamos?
dialog.en: How about dinner at the market and then a walk?

dialog.es: Me late la idea. ¿A qué hora?
dialog.en: I like that idea. What time?

dialog.es: Como a las siete, para agarrar mesa.
dialog.en: Around seven, so we can get a table.
Perfect, see you there.

spanish.use: Say it when a friend proposes a plan and you like it.

spanish.note: A very common Mexican way to say yes to a plan. Órale is an all-purpose exclamation (alright, wow, come on) and va means 'it's on'.

dialog.es: ¿Nos vemos a las siete para unos tacos?
dialog.en: Want to meet at seven for tacos?
Alright, let's do it!

dialog.es: Yo llego primero y pido mesa.
dialog.en: I'll get there first and get a table.
Perfect, see you there.

spanish.use: Say it when a friend proposes a plan and you are in.

spanish.meaning: Can you give me a hand?
spanish.note: Literally 'do you throw me the hand?'. Everyday Mexican for asking for help, from carrying boxes to fixing a problem.

cards.en: Give me a hand with this
Can I help you with something?

dialog.es: Voy a mover este sillón y está bien pesado.
dialog.en: I'm going to move this couch and it's really heavy.
Can you give me a hand?
Sure, where do I grab it?

dialog.es: Tú de ese lado, yo de este.
dialog.en: You on that side, me on this one.

spanish.use: Say it to a friend or coworker when you need help with something that takes two people.

options: Can you give me a hand?

phrases: Ni modo, ya será para la próxima
Ahorita vengo, voy por unos tacos

dare.title: Make shakshuka from scratch
dare.why: Before the day gets going, warm olive oil in your widest pan, soften an onion and a pepper, then stir in cumin, paprika and a can of crushed tomatoes. Make four little wells, crack an egg into each, put a lid on for six minutes, and eat it straight from the pan with whatever bread you have. No recipe video: one taste-and-adjust is allowed.
dare.worth: Shakshuka looks like something a restaurant made and takes a single pan. Cooking a dish from the far side of the Mediterranean is the cheapest way to travel before breakfast.
